title: Hypocalcaemia (Acute)
clinicalScenario: Outline only. Planned scope: Symptomatic versus asymptomatic, ECG, intravenous and oral replacement, magnesium and vitamin D, causes. Candidate sources to verify: Society for Endocrinology emergency guidance on acute hypocalcaemia.

evidenceAudit.scope: Adult (over 18 years) Emergency Department (ED) and acute medical treatment of acute symptomatic hypocalcaemia, based on the Society for Endocrinology 2013 emergency guidance and a Scottish secondary care guideline (version 3.0, January 2025). Paediatric and chronic hypoparathyroidism care are outside this protocol. No Saudi national guideline was found.
findings: Full protocol rebuilt from the source dossier opened on 2026-10-21; exact source locations are recorded in each investigation and medicine row.
The original outline remains preserved; this additive version is non-current and pending clinical review.
unverifiedSections: Normal ranges other than adjusted calcium are typical adult values, not from the cited guidelines.
Symptoms, signs, precipitants, differentials and pathophysiology are standard clinical content and were not extracted line by line.

The 2013 Society for Endocrinology guidance was due annual review and may be out of date; its magnesium dose figures are internally inconsistent (6 g magnesium sulfate is about 50 mmol, not 24 mmol) and are not used here. Page numbers in the Scottish guideline were inferred from running headers.

The Scottish oral calcium doses are labelled unlicensed; UK brand names (Adcal, Calvive, Sandocal, Cacit) may not be sold in Saudi Arabia and Saudi Food and Drug Authority (SFDA) availability was not checked.
No Saudi national or Saudi Ministry of Health hypocalcaemia guideline was found; duration of IV calcium infusion and the stopping criteria were not stated.

The SmPC is a UK product (B. Braun) and the 2.25 and 2.23 mmol per 10 mL figures differ inside it; Saudi products and concentrations were not checked. The rate limit of 2 mL per minute is quoted in the SmPC from an NHS guideline.

Renal, hepatic and age adjustments for the drugs added in this revision are from manufacturer labels (UK Summary of Product Characteristics, US prescribing information and a New Zealand data sheet), not from Saudi Food and Drug Authority labels.

pathophysiology.summary: Hypocalcaemia is a low albumin-adjusted calcium. Symptoms usually start when adjusted calcium falls below about 1.9 mmol/L, depending on the speed of fall.
keyMechanisms: Common causes: thyroid or parathyroid surgery, hypoparathyroidism, vitamin D deficiency, malabsorption, renal impairment, bisphosphonates and low magnesium.
Low magnesium blocks parathyroid hormone release and action, so calcium often corrects when magnesium is replaced.
Low calcium increases neuromuscular excitability and prolongs the QT interval.

symptoms: Perioral and finger tingling, muscle cramps, carpopedal spasm, anxiety.
physicalSigns: Chvostek and Trousseau signs, tetany, hyperreflexia.
Seizure, laryngospasm, prolonged QT on the electrocardiogram (ECG).
redFlags: Adjusted calcium below 1.9 mmol/L or symptomatic at any level below normal.
Digoxin therapy or existing arrhythmia (continuous ECG monitoring during IV calcium).
precipitants: Recent thyroid or parathyroid surgery, malabsorption, renal impairment, bisphosphonate use, hypomagnesaemia.

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Normal calcium; resolves with breathing control
Low magnesium; calcium corrects after replacement

ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Exclude artefact and resample if in doubt; adjusted calcium may be invalid if albumin is below 15 or above 50 g/L

clinicalManagement.title: Immediate
actions: Confirm the result and exclude artefact.
Severe or symptomatic: this is a medical emergency; give intravenous calcium gluconate with ECG monitoring.
Never replace with calcium chloride 10%; it is not equivalent to calcium gluconate.

clinicalManagement.title: Ongoing
actions: Repeat the bolus until the patient is asymptomatic, then start an infusion if needed.
Check magnesium and potassium and replace magnesium first or together.
Start oral calcium and, where indicated, alfacalcidol.

clinicalManagement.title: Escalation
actions: Cardiac arrhythmia, digoxin, or ongoing symptoms: continuous ECG monitoring and senior review.

clinicalManagement.title: Disposition
actions: Admit severe or symptomatic hypocalcaemia; post-thyroidectomy patients with adjusted calcium above 2.1 mmol/L may be discharged with a recheck within one week.

regimens.patientGroup: Adults with severe or symptomatic hypocalcaemia
regimens.dose: 10–20 mL (2.2–4.4 mmol) of 10% calcium gluconate (10 mL = about 2.1–2.25 mmol calcium) diluted in 50–100 mL of glucose 5% or sodium chloride 0.9% (about 1 in 10 dilution)
regimens.route: IV through a good vein with the patient lying down; over 10 minutes, never faster than 2 mL (0.45 mmol) of 10% calcium gluconate per minute; do not inject into fat or tissue; intramuscular only if IV is impossible
regimens.duration: Until asymptomatic; the bolus may be repeated every 6 hours if needed; check serum calcium every 4–6 hours with intermittent dosing
adjustments: Avoid large volumes in end-stage renal failure or dialysis
contraindications: Digoxin or arrhythmia: use only if life-threatening, with continuous ECG and slower administration (for example 100 mL of glucose 5% over 20 minutes) and emergency arrhythmia treatment available

medicationPlan.note: Doses came from an external drafting tool and must be verified against the cited sources, Saudi Food and Drug Authority (SFDA) registration and the local hospital protocol before prescribing. Check hospital formulary.

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Adjusted calcium below 1.9 mmol/L, or symptomatic below the reference range

values: Below 1.9 mmol/L, urgent action after excluding artefact
10–20 mL 10% calcium gluconate in 50–100 mL glucose 5% over 10 minutes
10–20 mL in 50–100 mL glucose 5% or sodium chloride 0.9% over 10 minutes
100 mL in 1 L normal saline or glucose 5% at 50–100 mL/hour
100 mL in 1 L sodium chloride 0.9% or glucose 5% at 50–100 mL/hour
Must not be used for replacement
Sandocal 1000 two tablets twice daily; alternatives Adcal, Cacit, Calcichew Forte
Adcal 1500 mg three tablets twice daily or Calvive two tablets twice daily
0.25 mcg/day if persistent after 72 hours; 0.25–0.5 mcg/day in hypoparathyroidism
250 nanograms daily if persistent after 72 hours
24 mmol over 24 hours as 6 g magnesium sulfate (dose figures inconsistent in the source)
Treat magnesium first; refer to separate guideline

learningObjectives: Recognise symptomatic hypocalcaemia and give IV calcium gluconate safely.
Replace magnesium and plan oral therapy and follow-up.
pitfalls: Using calcium chloride 10% for routine replacement.
Over-treatment with active vitamin D causing hypercalcaemia.
keyPoints: Give 10–20 mL of 10% calcium gluconate over 10 minutes with ECG monitoring.
